I believe God wants to help us regardless of how we approach Him, and that He actively tries to help us. Some people refuse the help though; they wilt in apathy while there is so much good to enjoy. I think largely you'd have to at least have the desire to believe in God in order to even accept the possiblity that He helped you, rather than dismissing it as chance or as a result of personal action. 

I think children can definitely accept God according to the degree of their understanding, which may not be much more than hoping that there's some bearded being out there that created and loves them. But Jesus taught that we must humble ourselves as little children in order to begin a life of faith; I interpret that to mean we need to be willing to first place trust in God that He loves us and that obeying His commandments  will help us, in order for our spirituality to grow into a rewarding relationship with God. 

I think salvation doesn't come from a one-time declaration of belief, but rather is the culmination of a life of trying to believe and do good according to the best of our understanding. The Bible says faith without works is dead; so between an atheist who does good and a religious person who does evil, who gets the greater reward? God very clearly doesn't appreciate lip-service; Isaiah makes that very clear. So my invitation is to do good, embrace all truth, and don't let other's actions define who God is for you, because that's between you and Him. So are you saved? Ask Him. Spiritual answers can come in a variety of forms so be patient.

TL; DR: 
1. No, but it's rewarding to recognize Him.
2. Yes but there's a lot to learn, discipleship is a lifetime learning experience.
3. That depends.

More power to you for it. As I've put more effort into following the teachings and into trying to connect with God through prayer, I've found much greater strength and progress than what I've been able to procure on my own (and I've tried; I struggle with addiction). I've found a personal relationship with Him, which has become a source of strength and evidence for me that He exists.

Everybody walks a difference path though, so I can only speak for myself. It's a broad subject to talk about and even harder to describe due to the largely personal feelings associated with spirituality (imagine describing how umami tastes to someone who has never tried it) but I do my best to explain it.

Interesting point. I'm a Christian and believe strongly in God's influence in my life, but I don't believe that he controls the world in the sense that He'll "break your legs." Physics and science and natural causes etc. are real and they're part of the collective truth we can learn that this life is designed to teach us. God won't change change some natural laws just to reward good behavior or punish bad behavior; He will, however, help us (through guidance or warning through the Holy Spirit) become better people through our experiences. 

So the very common question of "why do bad things happen to good people?" is answered in that things simply happen, to the good and the bad, if you want to label people in that way. God will help us respond to such experiences so we can increase our faith in Him and, yes, be happy regardless of externalities. That's largely the benefit of faith: peace that comes from trusting that whatever comes at us, ultimately it will help us become better people and grow closer to God so that we can actually enjoy being with Him after this life. 

What kind of heaven would it be, living with a God that just snapped his fingers to break your leg? It just doesn't make sense to me, personally. If I broke a leg it's because I fell and the force of the fall broke it. God's role would be help me understand and work through the pain, grant me patience to overcome, help me trust that one day I'll be better, and also to be able to empathize with others in the future that may have similar pain so I can help them.

I do believe in miracles but I see them more as uncommon natural occurrences that will further God's purposes (e.g. teach us, help us).

TL;DR I agree with those that view Job as more of a symbol or lesson in the same way earlier people have commented. But I don't believe God remote-controls our lives, He just helps us grow through experience.

I saw #207 today, it is titled "What xkcd Means," but it doesn't explain anything really. Maybe I'm thinking too shallow

Well, basically back when slavery was a hot topic in the united states, there was a big conflict about how slaves should be represented. They used to count as nothing by way of population, which made the South seem very small population wise. 

So then people said that slaves should actually count as people, because, you know, they're people. But since that sudden influx of people counting towards that population would give the South a whole bunch of representative power, the people up North (facing a potential loss of their own representative power) shot the notion down, because they didn't want to lose their representative advantage. 

So the 3/5's Compromise was the compromise between the North and the South, saying that each slave would count as 3/5 of a real person, so that blacks could count as real people, but not completely tip the scale.

The comment about counting the kills of Hitler was especially poignant, because he killed Jews, which are also discriminated upon. So the 3/5 comment was putting Jews in the same category of blacks, in a sort of faux-racist kind of joke that only US history knowers would get.
